pedagogy.summary: This is the conceptual heart of the strand: understanding that a ratio expresses a MULTIPLICATIVE relationship between two quantities — one is always a constant number of times the other — and that this same relationship can be written as a ratio (a:b), as a fraction (a/b), and as a linear function (y = (a/b)x) whose graph is a straight line through the origin. The learning goal is to see these as one idea in three costumes, and above all to distinguish a multiplicative relationship (constant ratio) from an additive one (constant difference). Teaching should surface the invariant — what stays the same as the quantities grow — using ratio tables, double number lines and graphs, and should repeatedly contrast 'so many times as' against 'so much more than'.
bestPractices: Foreground the invariant: as both quantities scale, the DIFFERENCE changes but the MULTIPLE stays constant — make 'how many times' the thing children look for.
Move fluently between the three representations on one example: ratio 1:3, fraction 1/3 (or 3 times), and y = 3x graphed as a line through the origin — name them as the same relationship.
Use a ratio table and read it both ways: down the columns (scaling, the multiplier) and across (the constant a:b relationship / the y = kx rule).
Directly contrast multiplicative and additive tables side by side (one where y = 3x, one where y = x + 4) and ask which is a ratio relationship and why.
Connect the straight-line-through-the-origin graph to proportionality: doubling x doubles y only when the line passes through (0,0).
Ground the abstraction in a perceptible constant-ratio context (paint shade, concentration, speed) so 'same relationship' is something the child can see or taste, not just assert.
keyRepresentations: Ratio table with the constant multiplier visible down the columns and the a:b relationship across
Double number line aligned at 0 (equal ratios line up)
Straight-line graph through the origin (y = kx) with gradient = the ratio
Paired multiplicative vs additive tables for contrast (y = 3x vs y = x + 4)
commonMisconceptions: Reads a relationship additively — fixes on the difference between a pair of values ('y is 4 more than x') instead of the constant multiple
Sees the constant multiplier for whole-number rows but cannot express it as a ratio, fraction, or y = kx
Confuses the part-to-part ratio a:b with the fraction a/b of the whole
Thinks any straight-line graph shows proportionality, not noticing it must pass through the origin

learn.summary: Learners come to see a ratio as a MULTIPLICATIVE relationship — one quantity is always a constant number of times the other — and to recognise this same relationship in three forms: a ratio a:b, a fraction a/b (x is a/b of y), and a linear function y=kx whose constant multiple k is the gradient and whose graph is a straight line through the origin. For the worked ratio 1:3 (x:y), x is 1/3 of y and y=3x, where the gradient 3 is y÷x. The central work is distinguishing a multiplicative relationship (constant ratio/multiple) from an additive one (constant difference). Vary the quantities, surface what stays the same (the multiple), and read the invariant across ratio tables, double number lines, graphs and a perceptible context such as paint shade. Keep part-to-part ratio a:b (x is 1/3 OF y) distinct from part-to-whole fraction (x out of the total x+y).

activities.title: One ratio, three costumes — and what breaks under 'add 4'
feedback: If a learner says the bigger batch is darker because there is 'more red', have them test y÷x on each row: it is always 3, so the proportion of red is unchanged — only the total amount grew.

If a learner fixes on a single pair's difference (e.g. '2 to 6 is +4'), have them test +4 on the next rows: 9 would have to be 7 and 12 would have to be 8, so +4 fails — the difference is not constant.
When the additive toggle is on, point to the line lifting off (0,0) and the shifting shade as the visible signs that the relationship is no longer a constant ratio.
Confirm that '×3', '1:3', 'x is 1/3 of y' and 'y=3x' are all names for the same relationship, and that the straight line passes through the origin because when x=0, y=0.
activities.rationale: The defining feature of this concept is an invariant that is felt by varying the quantities and watching what stays the same; linking a table, a graph and a perceptible mixture lets the constant multiple, the fraction and the gradient move together under scaling and break together under an additive rule. Linked panels with live recolouring and a rule toggle are offered as one concrete way to make the mechanism visible, not as the only means; this is a proposed design, not a validated intervention.
sourceClaims: At KS3 pupils 'understand that a multiplicative relationship between two quantities can be expressed as a ratio or a fraction' and 'relate the language of ratios and the associated calculations to the arithmetic of fractions and to linear functions'.

NCETM names as a central misconception that 'students often assume that relationships are additive... in situations where the actual relationship is multiplicative', considering the difference a−b rather than the ratio a:b (e.g. assuming a ratio 2:5 means one share is always £3 more than the other). It presents the one structure x×k=y expressible as ratio, fraction and the linear function y=mx (a straight line through the origin), and distinguishes scalar from functional multipliers using ratio tables and double number lines (which must both start at aligned zeros).
learnerActions: Work with the ratio 1:3 (e.g. red:yellow paint) and extend a ratio table: 1:3, 2:6, 3:9, 4:12, scaling both quantities together.
For each new row, plot the point (x,y) on a coordinate graph and note that the points fall on a straight line passing through the origin (0,0).
Observe a perceptible constant-ratio context alongside: in an idealised, thoroughly mixed model, a paint swatch mixed in that ratio keeps the same orange shade as the batch grows.
Name the same relationship in three forms on this one example: ratio 1:3, fraction/multiple (y is 3 times x; x is 1/3 of y), and linear function y=3x with gradient 3 (the gradient equals y÷x).

Switch the rule from multiplicative (y=3x) to additive (y=x+4) and watch what changes: the graph's line no longer passes through the origin, the plotted points leave the straight proportional line, and the swatch shade shifts row by row.
State in your own words which quantity stays constant in each case — the MULTIPLE stays fixed for a ratio relationship, while the DIFFERENCE stays fixed for an additive one.
activities.intendedInsight: A ratio is a single multiplicative idea wearing three costumes (ratio a:b, fraction a/b, straight line y=kx through the origin); its signature is a constant multiple, not a constant difference. When the quantities scale, the difference changes but the multiple — and the colour, the ratio and the gradient — stay the same. An additive rule breaks the line-through-origin and changes the shade, which is what separates it from a ratio.

activities.title: Read the ratio table both ways
feedback: If a learner extends row by row to reach x=10, prompt them to use the ×3 multiplier directly: 10×3=30.
If a learner writes the fraction using the total as denominator (e.g. 2/8 for x:y=2:6), separate the readings: the ratio compares x to y (x is 1/3 of y); part-to-whole would compare x to x+y=8.
Confirm a double number line only shows equal ratios when both lines start at aligned zeros.
activities.rationale: Reading a ratio table down (scalar) and across (functional), with an aligned double number line, is the representation NCETM uses to distinguish scalar from functional multipliers; keeping part-to-part separate from part-to-whole addresses a documented confusion. These are proposed uses of standard representations, not tested interventions.
sourceClaims: NCETM names as a central misconception that 'students often assume that relationships are additive... in situations where the actual relationship is multiplicative', considering the difference a−b rather than the ratio a:b (e.g. assuming a ratio 2:5 means one share is always £3 more than the other). It presents the one structure x×k=y expressible as ratio, fraction and the linear function y=mx (a straight line through the origin), and distinguishes scalar from functional multipliers using ratio tables and double number lines (which must both start at aligned zeros).
learnerActions: Take a ratio table and read DOWN the columns to find the scalar multiplier (how each row scales from the previous).
Read ACROSS the rows to find the constant functional relationship a:b / the y=kx rule between the two quantities.
Use a double number line aligned at 0 so that equal ratios line up, and check that both lines start at aligned zeros.
Given x=10 for a 1:3 relationship, work out y directly using the multiplier (×3) rather than extending the table row by row.

Distinguish 'x is 1/3 OF y' (part-to-part, the correct multiplicative reading) from 'x is a fraction of the whole x+y' (part-to-whole); for example, with 2 red : 5 blue beads, red is 2/5 of the blue count (part-to-part) but 2 out of 7 total beads (part-to-whole), anchoring each reading to its own picture.
activities.intendedInsight: A ratio table encodes both a scalar multiplier (down columns) and a functional multiplier (across, the y=kx rule); the multiple can be used directly to predict any value. A double number line aligned at zero shows equal ratios lining up. Part-to-part and part-to-whole are different comparisons.

activities.title: Sort and match: is it a ratio relationship?
feedback: For the x=2,y=5 / x=4,y=7 table, if a learner calls it a ratio, have them compute 5÷2=2.5 and 7÷4=1.75: the multiple is not constant, so it is additive (+3), not a ratio.
If a learner picks any straight line as proportional, ask where it crosses the y-axis: only a line through (0,0) represents y=kx.
When a learner matches 1:3 to y=3x, ask them to confirm the gradient of the line equals the multiple (3).
activities.rationale: Distinguishing multiplicative from additive tables and translating between forms can be checked with sorting, matching and prediction tasks using additive distractors. A sort can check classification and translation but does not itself require the learner to construct the invariant by varying quantities, so pair it with the manipulation activity above.
sourceClaims: At KS3 pupils 'understand that a multiplicative relationship between two quantities can be expressed as a ratio or a fraction' and 'relate the language of ratios and the associated calculations to the arithmetic of fractions and to linear functions'.
learnerActions: Sort several tables of values into 'ratio relationship' vs 'not a ratio relationship', justifying each by whether y÷x is constant.
Match equivalent forms: connect 1:3 with y=3x and with a straight line through the origin.
Predict y for a new x in a given table, with an additive answer offered as a tempting but wrong option, and explain why the additive choice fails.
Given two graphs, identify which shows proportionality and explain that it must pass through the origin.
Test a tricky table — x=2,y=5 and x=4,y=7 — and decide whether it is a ratio relationship (it is additive: +3 each time, but 5÷2 ≠ 7÷4, so no constant multiple).
activities.intendedInsight: Sorting and matching across forms, with deliberate additive distractors, can check whether a learner can translate among ratio, fraction and linear form and can reject an additive table as not proportional. A straight-line graph only shows proportionality when it passes through the origin.

activities.title: Justify it: times or more than?
feedback: If the learner reasons 'more red so darker' or 'different amounts so different', treat this as additive/absolute-amount reasoning and have them predict then check against y÷x.
Accept a full explanation only when it names the constant multiple AND notes that the difference is not constant.
Use the predict-observe-explain paint task so the reason stated before mixing is the diagnostic part.
activities.rationale: A Socratic challenge with a scaled counter-case targets the additive-vs-multiplicative distinction directly. Verbal justification can complement seeing the invariant across linked representations; use it alongside the manipulation activity rather than in place of it.
sourceClaims: NCETM names as a central misconception that 'students often assume that relationships are additive... in situations where the actual relationship is multiplicative', considering the difference a−b rather than the ratio a:b (e.g. assuming a ratio 2:5 means one share is always £3 more than the other). It presents the one structure x×k=y expressible as ratio, fraction and the linear function y=mx (a straight line through the origin), and distinguishes scalar from functional multipliers using ratio tables and double number lines (which must both start at aligned zeros).
learnerActions: Face a mentor who presents tables and asks for each: 'is it times, or more than? How do you know?'
Defend your classification by pointing to the constant multiple and showing that the difference changes down the table.
Respond to a scaled counter-case when you give an additive answer — e.g. 'you said +4; check the next row, does +4 still work?'
Explain, before mixing any paint, whether a 2:6 batch will be darker, lighter or the same shade as a 1:3 batch, and why.
activities.intendedInsight: Being pressed to justify whether a relationship is multiplicative or additive, and to meet a scaled counter-case, brings the reasoning into the open and can check whether the learner gives the right answer for the right reason.

constraints: Target age 12–14 (KS3); this is a conceptual objective about ratio notation and multiplicative relationships.
Ground the abstraction in at least one perceptible constant-ratio context (paint shade, concentration, speed) so 'same relationship' can be seen, not merely asserted.

The invariant is best surfaced by varying values and watching what stays fixed; a static annotated triple (table, ratio, graph) can summarise and reference the connections but does not itself let the learner vary quantities, so use it as a summary rather than the sole discovery activity.

Sorting, matching and prediction tasks can check and consolidate translation between forms but are recognition-level; they do not by themselves require independent construction of the invariant, so pair them with activities where the learner scales the quantities and states the relationship.

Express the linear form as y=kx where k (the gradient) is the constant multiple y÷x; for ratio 1:3 that is y=3x. Do not write the gradient as a/b (which for 1:3 would give the incorrect 1/3); a/b=1/3 is the separate fraction reading 'x is 1/3 of y'.
Keep part-to-part ratio a:b ('x is 1/3 OF y') distinct from part-to-whole fraction (x out of total x+y); do not let learners write the fraction with the total as denominator.
Double number lines must start at aligned zeros for equal ratios to line up; a ratio table does not need a 0:0 row, though including one can show the link to the origin on the graph.
A straight-line graph shows proportionality only when it passes through the origin; a line not through (0,0) represents y=kx+c, not a ratio relationship.

Live recolouring, a rule toggle (y=3x vs y=x+4), draggable/extendable table rows and linked plotting are offered as optional ways to make the mechanism concrete; they are examples of interaction, not required mechanisms.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original row expressed the linear function both as 'y=(a/b)x' and as the triple '1:3 = y=3x'. These are inconsistent: for the ratio a:b = 1:3 (x:y), the gradient is y÷x = b/a = 3, so y=3x, whereas y=(a/b)x gives the incorrect y=(1/3)x. The guidance has been corrected to state y=kx with gradient = y÷x; the original formula is recorded as an error, not offered to learners.

The legacy row rated a 3D artefact 'poor' with the claim '3D adds nothing'. This comparative/necessity claim is not established by the cited sources and has been dropped; the relationship is primarily numeric/graphical, a reasonable scoping note, but no universal medium superiority is implied.
The legacy framing that the linked-panel tool is uniquely able to teach the concept has been softened: linked panels are one concrete way to expose the invariant, not the only way.

Arithmetic self-audit: for the counter-case table x=2,y=5 and x=4,y=7 the differences are +3 (5−2 and 7−4); the ratios 5÷2=2.5 and 7÷4=1.75 are unequal, confirming it is additive, not a ratio. For the 1:3 relationship, rows 2:6, 3:9, 4:12 give y÷x=3 throughout with differences 4,6,8 (not constant), confirming multiplicative. x=10 gives y=30. For the bead example 2 red : 5 blue, the total is 7, so part-to-whole red is 2/7, distinct from the part-to-part reading 2/5.

The original assess 'additive' distractor 'y is always 4 more than x' refers to the first pair 2→6 (difference 4); it is retained only as a diagnostic distractor to be challenged, never taught as correct.
The original part-to-whole distractor 'x is 2 out of the whole 8, so the relationship is 2/8' is retained only as a misconception to separate and correct, not as a valid reading.
Whether any of these proposed activities improve learning is untested; sources support the curriculum content and the additive misconception, not the specific interventions.

assess.poeTask: Show the child a jar of orange paint made from 1 spoon red and 3 spoons yellow, and a second, bigger batch you will make from 2 spoons red and 6 spoons yellow. PREDICT before mixing: will the bigger batch be a darker orange, a lighter orange, or exactly the same shade — and WHY? (A child reasoning 'more red, so darker' or 'different amounts, so different' is reasoning additively/by absolute amount; the reason stated before mixing is the diagnostic part.) OBSERVE: mix both — the shades match exactly. EXPLAIN: because 2:6 is the same ratio as 1:3 (both parts multiplied by 2), the multiplicative relationship — and so the colour — is unchanged; adding different amounts to each part is what would change the shade.
probeDeeper: 'Write this relationship as a ratio x:y, and as y = ? × x' — checks the translation among ratio, fraction and linear form.

Counterexample: 'Another table has x = 2, y = 5 and x = 4, y = 7. Is THAT a ratio relationship? How do you know?' — this one is additive (+3, but 5÷2 ≠ 7÷4); a child with the concept identifies it as 'add', NOT a constant ratio.
'If x = 10, what is y — and how do you know without extending the table row by row?' — tests whether the multiplier is used directly.
'If we plotted these points, what would the graph look like, and why does it go through (0,0)?' — links proportionality to the line through the origin.
assess.correctAnswer: y is always the same number of TIMES x — y is 3 times x (y = 3x). You can tell because the AMOUNT bigger changes (6 is 4 more than 2, 9 is 6 more, 15 is 10 more) so it is not a constant 'more than', but y ÷ x is always 3, a constant multiple — this is the multiplicative relationship, the ratio x:y = 1:3.

errorPatterns.pattern: Additive: fixes on the difference in the first pair ('y is 4 more than x, because 2 and 6') and treats the relationship as constant addition
errorPatterns.nextMove: Have the child test '+4' on every row (9 would need to be 7; 15 would need to be 9) — the difference is not constant. Then find y÷x for each row (all 3) to surface the constant multiple. Documented additive-strategy interference.
errorPatterns.distractor: y is always 4 more than x
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child gives '+4' (or another single-row difference) and does not check it against the other rows, where it fails

errorPatterns.pattern: Confuses the part-to-part ratio with a part-to-whole fraction: reads x:y = 2:6 and says 'so x is 2/6... 1/3 of the whole' misapplying the fraction
errorPatterns.nextMove: Separate the two readings: the ratio compares x to y (x is 1/3 of y); part-to-whole would compare x to x+y. Anchor each to its own picture.
errorPatterns.distractor: x is 2 out of the whole 8, so the relationship is 2/8
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child mixes up 'x is 1/3 OF y' (correct multiplicative reading) with 'x is 1/3 of the whole' (part-to-whole), or writes the fraction with the total 8 as denominator

errorPatterns.pattern: Sees the ×3 for the whole-number rows but cannot express the relationship as a ratio, a fraction, or y = 3x
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do not reteach the concept — scaffold the notation link: 'times 3' = ratio 1:3 = y = 3x; connect to the straight-line-through-origin graph. The idea is present; the representations need joining.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child says 'times 3' correctly but cannot write it as 1:3 or y = 3x when asked

responseLevels.gap: Reads the relationship additively (a constant 'more than') and cannot see that the difference changes; treats one pair's difference as the rule.
responseLevels.full: States that y is a constant number of times x, justifies it by the changing difference vs constant multiple, expresses the relationship as 1:3, 1/3 and y = 3x, links it to a straight line through the origin, and correctly rejects an additive table as not a ratio relationship.
responseLevels.partial: Identifies the constant multiple (×3) for the given rows but cannot yet express it as a ratio/fraction/linear function, or slips between part-to-part and part-to-whole, or does not connect it to the line through the origin — knows the pieces without coordinating them.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here is a table of matching values. When x = 2, y = 6; when x = 3, y = 9; when x = 5, y = 15. I want two things. First: is y always the same AMOUNT bigger than x, or always the same number of TIMES x? Second, and most important: how can you tell from the table which one it is?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Asking for the REASON (tier two), not just the classification, is what separates genuine multiplicative understanding from a guess. A child reasoning multiplicatively points to the constant multiple (3) and notes the difference is NOT constant; a child reasoning additively latches onto one pair's difference (2 to 6 is +4) and cannot see that the +4 fails on the next row. Because the 'amount bigger' visibly changes down the table while the multiple stays fixed, a correct answer is hard to give for the wrong reason and a wrong answer is hard to give for the right reason.
